explanations.c: The shared authentication infrastructure creates a legitimate scope consideration: (1) Shared identity provider risk: if production and development use the same Active Directory, Okta, or other identity provider — a developer account misconfiguration or privilege escalation in development could potentially be used to access production systems; an attacker compromising a developer's credentials gains production access if authentication is shared; (2) Change management boundary: if developers can deploy code from development to production through the shared infrastructure without segregation, the change management control environment is at risk; (3) Scope assessment: the shared infrastructure components (identity provider, authentication servers) should be within scope; the development code environment itself may remain out of scope if properly isolated; (4) Controls to evaluate: segregation between development and production accounts; access controls preventing development roles from accessing production data; monitoring of privileged access through the shared identity system; (5) SOC 2 guidance: the system boundary should include all infrastructure whose controls affect the service organization's ability to meet its commitments — shared authentication clearly meets this criterion.
explanations.d: Scope decisions are driven by security relevance and the nature of the service — cost considerations are separate. Including shared infrastructure components is a professional judgment about risk, not a fee negotiation.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Understanding system boundaries in SOC 2 — scope, system components, and service org definitions
questions.text: During a SOC 2 engagement, the service auditor is comparing the service organization's system description to the actual system to evaluate whether the description is complete. The description identifies the system boundary as including three data centers. Testing reveals that the service organization also uses a fourth data center to process customer data during peak periods, but this facility is not mentioned in the system description. How should the service auditor address this?

answers.text: Accept the description as complete — the three primary data centers represent the core of the system; a fourth facility used only during peak periods is immaterial by definition
Exclude the fourth data center from the engagement entirely — the service auditor tests only what management has described, not what exists in practice

The fourth data center is a component of the system as operated that is not reflected in the system description — if it processes customer data, it is within the system boundary and should be included in the description; the service auditor should request management to update the description and should evaluate the controls at the fourth data center, noting any gap if it cannot be evaluated
Issue a separate supplemental report covering the fourth data center — systems not in the main description require standalone attestation

explanations.a: 'Used only during peak periods' does not make a facility immaterial if it processes actual customer data. A data center handling customer data has controls (physical security, environmental controls, logical access) that affect the service organization's ability to meet its security and availability commitments. The frequency of use doesn't determine whether its controls matter.
explanations.b: The service auditor's responsibility includes evaluating whether the description fairly presents the actual system — which requires awareness of actual operations, not just what management has documented. Limiting testing to only what's in the description when the auditor knows it's incomplete would be inadequate.
explanations.c: System description completeness and the omitted facility: (1) Description completeness requirement: management's assertion covers that the description 'fairly presents the service organization's system' — omitting a facility that processes customer data means the description is incomplete; (2) Customer data processing scope: any infrastructure that processes, stores, or transmits customer data is within the system boundary — the fourth data center processes customer data during peak periods, making it a system component; (3) Service auditor's obligation: report the description incompleteness — the description doesn't fairly present the system; require management to update the description to include the fourth data center; evaluate the controls at the fourth data center (or note if access is denied) — user entities need assurance about ALL facilities processing their data, not just three of four; (4) Testing gap: if the fourth data center was not evaluated, the service auditor cannot provide complete assurance that customer data is protected across all processing locations; this may affect the scope of the opinion.
explanations.d: Supplemental reports for undisclosed components are not standard practice — the appropriate resolution is to update the primary system description and expand the evaluation scope.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Understanding system boundaries in SOC 2 — scope, system components, and service org definitions
questions.text: A service organization provides two distinct services: (1) cloud storage and (2) cloud-based payroll processing. The services use separate infrastructure and have different user entity bases. Management proposes a single SOC 2 covering both services to reduce cost. An IS auditor advises considering separate reports. Which argument MOST effectively supports the separate-reports approach?

answers.text: Combining services always violates SOC 2 standards — one report per service is a mandatory AICPA requirement

A combined report covering both services may be appropriate only if they share significant infrastructure and controls; combining two services with separate infrastructure and distinct user bases into one report could confuse user entities (cloud storage users don't need the payroll SOC 2), add unnecessary scope for each user entity's assessment, and potentially dilute the specificity of each service's system description; separate reports better serve each distinct user base's needs
Separate reports are required because the services have different pricing — each revenue stream requires its own attestation
The cost argument is irrelevant — the service auditor should always recommend the most expensive engagement option to maximize professional fees

explanations.a: AICPA standards do not mandate one report per service — combined reports for related services are permitted. The professional judgment question is whether a combined report serves users appropriately given the specific circumstances.
explanations.b: Analysis of combined vs. separate SOC 2 reports: Combined report appropriate when: services share significant infrastructure (same servers, networks, authentication); the user base substantially overlaps; the controls for both services are largely the same. Separate reports appropriate when (this scenario): services have separate infrastructure — controls evaluated are largely distinct for each service; distinct user bases — cloud storage users have no need to review payroll processing controls; they would receive an unnecessarily large, confusing report covering systems they don't use; payroll users receiving the combined report see cloud storage controls that are irrelevant to their risk assessment; assessment burden — user entity auditors must review the entire combined report to understand what applies to their client's use case; separate reports are cleaner and more targeted; confidentiality — combining the services may expose payroll user entities to information about cloud storage services that isn't relevant to them and vice versa. Management's cost concern can be partially addressed by the service auditor offering efficiencies in testing two separate engagements simultaneously (shared fieldwork where controls overlap). The professional recommendation should prioritize user entity utility.
explanations.c: Revenue pricing has no relevance to SOC 2 report structure. The determination is based on service organization structure, user base needs, and control environment — not financial arrangements.
explanations.d: Professional recommendations should prioritize client and user entity interests — maximizing engagement fees is not the decision criterion. The recommendation should be based on what best serves the SOC 2's purpose: providing meaningful assurance to user entities.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Communication of failures, incidents, and complaints in SOC 2 engagements
questions.text: Under the AICPA Trust Services Criteria, the service organization is required to provide user entities with information about system incidents. Which Trust Services criterion MOST directly addresses this communication requirement?

answers.text: CC1.1 — The entity demonstrates a commitment to integrity and ethical values
CC4.1 — The entity selects, develops, and performs ongoing and/or separate evaluations to ascertain whether the components of internal control are present and functioning

CC9.2 — The entity assesses and manages risks associated with service disruptions — combined with the Availability criterion A1.3 requiring the service organization to maintain procedures to provide user entities with information about system incidents and complaints
CC7.4 — The entity communicates information about system incidents to affected parties to respond to and recover from incidents

explanations.a: CC1.1 addresses the control environment component — ethical values and commitment to integrity. While this foundational principle indirectly supports all communications, it does not specifically address the requirement to communicate system incidents to user entities.
explanations.b: CC4.1 addresses monitoring activities — ongoing and separate evaluations to assess whether controls are present and functioning. Monitoring relates to internal oversight, not the communication of incidents to external user entities.
explanations.c: CC9.2 addresses risk management in supply chain and vendor relationships. While availability criterion A1.3 does address providing user entities with availability information, the most direct criterion for communicating security incidents to affected parties is in the CC7 (System Operations and Incident Management) series.
explanations.d: CC7.4 under the Common Criteria (CC7 System Operations) specifically addresses incident communication: the entity communicates information about system incidents to affected parties including: notification when incidents occur that could affect user entities' ability to use the service; providing timely updates about incident status, impact, and resolution; communicating root cause and remediation actions after incidents are resolved; this criterion directly implements the service organization's obligation to keep user entities informed about security and operational incidents that affect the service they receive.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Communication of failures, incidents, and complaints in SOC 2 engagements
questions.text: A service organization's SOC 2 system description states: 'The service organization has established a process for communicating system incidents to affected user entities within 4 hours of incident identification.' During testing, the service auditor reviews incident logs and finds three incidents during the period where notifications were sent 6-12 hours after incident identification. How should these findings be reflected in the SOC 2 report?

answers.text: The findings should not be reported — communication delays are common operational issues that do not rise to the level of SOC 2 exceptions

The three instances where notification exceeded the 4-hour commitment should be reported as operating effectiveness exceptions — the control (4-hour notification) did not operate as described in three instances; the service auditor should include these in the noted exceptions section of the report with the nature and number of exceptions
Only one exception should be reported regardless of the number of instances — SOC 2 reports are limited to identifying a single exception per control
The exceptions should be reported only if any user entity was harmed by the delayed notification — absent demonstrated harm, exceptions are not reported

explanations.a: Communication delay exceptions are reportable in SOC 2 — the service organization made a specific commitment (4-hour notification) and that commitment was not met in three documented instances. These are operating effectiveness exceptions under CC7.4 (incident communication) and potentially the Availability criterion. Operational commonality does not exempt exceptions from reporting.
explanations.b: Exception reporting for notification delays: (1) The control tested: notifying affected user entities within 4 hours of incident identification — a specific, testable commitment; (2) Exception identification: 6-12 hour notifications in 3 instances vs. 4-hour commitment = deviation from stated control; (3) SOC 2 report treatment: include in the exceptions section: control description: 'notification within 4 hours of incident identification'; testing performed: reviewed incident log for N incidents; exception: in 3 of N incidents, notification occurred 6-12 hours after identification; (4) Management response: management may include a response explaining: root cause (notifications were delayed because the on-call engineer was unavailable during one incident; escalation procedure failed); remediation: updated on-call procedures, automated notification system implemented; (5) User entity impact: user entities receiving the SOC 2 can evaluate whether 6-12 hour notification delays affected their own incident response planning; (6) Opinion impact: 3 exceptions in the notification control may or may not affect the overall opinion depending on the materiality assessment.
explanations.c: SOC 2 reports can and do identify multiple exceptions within the same control — the report describes each exception's nature and frequency. There is no limit of one exception per control.
explanations.d: SOC 2 exceptions are reported based on whether controls operated as described — demonstrated harm to user entities is not a prerequisite for exception reporting. A delayed notification that didn't cause harm in a specific case is still an exception to the stated control commitment.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Communication of failures, incidents, and complaints in SOC 2 engagements
questions.text: A service organization performs a SOC 2 walkthrough related to how the organization provides user entities with a means to report failures, incidents, and complaints related to the system. The service auditor asks management to demonstrate the process. Management shows a generic customer support email address. The IS auditor identifies a potential gap. Which concern is MOST valid?

answers.text: No concern — a generic support email is a standard and adequate mechanism for receiving all types of user entity communications including security incidents

A generic customer support email may be inadequate for receiving security incidents and system failures — security incidents often require dedicated reporting channels (security@, a dedicated incident portal) with different handling procedures than general customer support; complaints about a billing error and reports of a suspected data breach require very different response processes, timeframes, and escalation paths; a single generic email without differentiated handling procedures may result in security incidents being handled as routine support tickets rather than receiving the priority and specialized response they require
The concern is only about email server reliability — the service organization should use a redundant email system to prevent missed communications
Generic email addresses are prohibited in SOC 2 — the Trust Services Criteria require dedicated portals for incident reporting

explanations.a: A generic support email may technically provide a mechanism for communication, but it may not provide an adequate mechanism specifically for security incidents and system failures — which have different urgency, handling, and escalation requirements than routine service questions.
explanations.b: Differentiated incident reporting gap: (1) Distinct communication categories: billing question → low urgency, support team, standard resolution; service disruption complaint → medium urgency, operations team, service credit processing; suspected data breach or security incident → high urgency, security team + legal + potentially regulatory authorities, incident response activation; (2) Problems with single generic email: routing — all messages go to general support queue; triaging — a security incident email may sit in the queue waiting for a support rep to recognize its significance; escalation — generic support teams may not know the escalation path for security incidents; response time — generic support SLAs (48 hours) may not meet the incident response urgency (immediate); (3) What the Trust Services Criteria require (CC7.4, A1.3): the service organization must have a process for receiving and responding to incidents and complaints from user entities — a well-functioning process includes: dedicated reporting channels for security events; defined intake procedures; clear escalation to appropriate personnel; documented response SLAs differentiated by severity; (4) Recommended improvement: dedicated security incident reporting channel (security@company.com or a ticketing portal with incident category) with documented handling procedures.
explanations.c: Email server reliability is a separate availability consideration — the concern here is whether the reporting mechanism is appropriately designed for the type of communications it receives, not whether the email server might fail.
explanations.d: The Trust Services Criteria require an effective mechanism — they do not specify that dedicated portals are required over email. However, the criteria require that the mechanism be appropriate for the type of communications received.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Communication of failures, incidents, and complaints in SOC 2 engagements
questions.text: An IS auditor reviews a service organization's process for communicating system failures and incidents to user entities. The service organization's system description states it provides 'timely notification' of incidents. During testing, the service auditor finds: (1) three incidents were communicated within 2 hours; (2) two incidents were communicated within 4 hours; and (3) one incident took 11 days to communicate because management was uncertain whether notification was required. Which combined finding is MOST significant, and why?

answers.text: Finding 3 (11-day delay) is the most significant — the extreme delay suggests a systemic problem with management's decision-making process for incident notification, potentially indicating that the communication commitment in the system description is not reliably met when management exercises discretion
Findings 1 and 2 are most significant — the variability between 2-hour and 4-hour notification times indicates an inconsistent communication process that warrants immediate remediation
All findings are equally significant — any deviation from a stated commitment is a material exception regardless of degree
None of the findings is significant — 'timely notification' is subjective and 11 days may be within subjective interpretation of 'timely'

explanations.a: Finding 3 analysis: (1) 11-day delay: even interpreting 'timely' generously (hours to days for urgent notifications), 11 days is well outside any reasonable definition of timely for a system incident; (2) Root cause significance: the stated reason ('uncertain whether notification was required') indicates a process deficiency more serious than execution failure — management had uncertainty about whether to notify at all; this suggests: absence of clear criteria for what constitutes a notifiable incident; no escalation process for uncertain cases; potential pattern of under-notifying user entities when management exercises discretion about notification obligation; (3) Systemic vs. isolated: findings 1 and 2 (2-hour vs. 4-hour) show normal process variation within a reasonable timeframe — likely isolated execution differences; finding 3 reveals a process design gap — unclear decision criteria and excessive management discretion over notification; (4) User entity impact: an 11-day delay in receiving notification of a system incident could seriously affect: user entity's own incident response; regulatory notification timelines (if the incident involved personal data, GDPR 72-hour clock may have started); risk assessment and compensating controls for the period of unknown incident; (5) SOC 2 significance: finding 3 would be highlighted as the most significant exception in the test results; the service auditor should evaluate whether the notification process meets the CC7.4 and Availability criteria given this gap.
explanations.b: 2-hour vs. 4-hour variations within the same incident period are normal process execution differences — neither represents a problematic delay for system incident notification. The variability is within a range that most user entities would consider timely. These findings do not indicate a systemic problem.
explanations.c: Not all deviations are equal regardless of degree — finding 3 (11 days, with a process confusion root cause) is categorically more significant than findings 1 and 2 (execution differences within a reasonable range). Professional judgment requires evaluating the nature and magnitude of exceptions, not treating all deviations as equivalent.
explanations.d: 'Timely' is not infinitely elastic — while it lacks a specific hour requirement in the system description, industry norms and user entity expectations establish that system incident notification within hours to a day or two is timely. 11 days is not a reasonable interpretation of 'timely' in the context of system incidents affecting user entities' operations.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts — impact on SOC 1 and SOC 2 engagements
questions.text: In the context of SOC engagements, which statement BEST describes a 'subsequent event'?

answers.text: A subsequent event is a control exception that occurs during the engagement period but is only detected by the service auditor after testing is complete

A subsequent event is an event that occurs after the period covered by the SOC report (the 'as of date' for Type 1 or the 'period end date' for Type 2) but before the service auditor's report is issued — it may require disclosure in the report if it is of sufficient significance
A subsequent event is a new service that the service organization launches after the SOC report is issued — user entities must request a supplemental report to cover the new service
Subsequent events do not apply in SOC engagements — the concept is unique to financial statement audits

explanations.a: A control exception occurring during the engagement period is within the scope of the SOC report and would be included in the regular test results — it is not a 'subsequent event.' Subsequent events specifically refer to events after the coverage period ends.
explanations.b: Subsequent events in SOC engagements: (1) Timing: a Type 1 SOC report has an 'as of date' (e.g., December 31) — subsequent events occur after December 31 but before the report is issued (e.g., February 15 when the report is signed); a Type 2 SOC report has a period end date (e.g., December 31) — subsequent events occur after December 31 but before report issuance; (2) Relevance: subsequent events that are significant enough to affect user entities' understanding of the system or the service auditor's conclusions should be disclosed; (3) Types of significant subsequent events: a significant breach discovered after period end but before report issuance; a system failure that calls into question the control environment; management personnel changes affecting key controls; acquisition or divestiture affecting the system boundary; material changes to the system that would have changed the report if they had occurred during the period; (4) Disclosure: significant subsequent events are disclosed in the SOC report (typically in a separate section) with appropriate description of the event and its nature.
explanations.c: New service launches after report issuance are not subsequent events that require supplemental reports — they are changes to the service organization's offerings that would be covered in the next SOC engagement cycle.
explanations.d: Subsequent event concepts apply to attestation engagements including SOC 1 and SOC 2. The AICPA's attestation standards (AT-C Section 205) address subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts in attestation engagements.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts — impact on SOC 1 and SOC 2 engagements
questions.text: A SOC 2 Type 2 engagement covers January 1 through December 31. The service auditor completes testing and begins drafting the report in January of the following year. On February 1, before the report is issued, the service organization suffers a ransomware attack that encrypts its primary database. The attack appears to exploit a vulnerability that existed during the engagement period but was not identified during testing. How should the service auditor address this subsequent event?

answers.text: Ignore the ransomware attack — it occurred after the engagement period (December 31) and therefore has no relevance to the SOC 2 report

The ransomware attack is a subsequent event that should be disclosed in the SOC 2 report — particularly because it suggests a vulnerability may have existed during the engagement period; the service auditor should: investigate whether the exploited vulnerability existed during the coverage period; assess whether additional testing is required to determine if controls were effective during the period; and disclose the subsequent event in the report if it is significant and potentially affects user entities' reliance on the report
The service auditor should issue the SOC 2 report without any reference to the ransomware attack and then issue a separate addendum report about the subsequent event
The service auditor must reopen the engagement and re-test all controls for the January 1 through December 31 period before issuing the report

explanations.a: Subsequent events are relevant to SOC reports when they are significant and potentially affect user entities' understanding or reliance. A ransomware attack exploiting a vulnerability that existed during the covered period directly affects the reliability of control conclusions for that period — it cannot be ignored.
explanations.b: Subsequent event disclosure and investigation: (1) Relevance determination: the attack exploits a vulnerability that 'existed during the engagement period' — this is critical; if the vulnerability was present during January 1 – December 31, it means controls may not have been as effective as the test results suggested; (2) Investigation required: the service auditor must determine: when did the vulnerability originate? Was it present during the engagement period? If so, was it detectable by the testing performed? Could it have been exploited during the period without detection? Does the subsequent attack indicate a control design or operating effectiveness gap that should have been reported?; (3) Report disclosure: if the investigation determines the vulnerability existed during the period and represents a material condition, the service auditor must disclose the subsequent event in the report — a subsequent event section describing the ransomware attack, the vulnerability, its timeline, and the impact on control conclusions; (4) If the vulnerability arose after December 31, it is a subsequent event that may warrant disclosure to inform user entities about the current state of the system, but does not affect the period's control conclusions; (5) User entity impact: user entities relying on the SOC 2 need to know about events that affect their confidence in the service organization's security posture.
explanations.c: A separate addendum report is not standard practice — significant subsequent events are disclosed within the primary SOC report in a subsequent events section. If the report has already been issued, different procedures apply (subsequently discovered facts).
explanations.d: Re-testing all controls for the prior period is not required for every subsequent event — the service auditor investigates the specific subsequent event's implications for the period's control conclusions and determines what additional procedures (if any) are needed.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts — impact on SOC 1 and SOC 2 engagements
questions.text: A SOC 2 Type 2 report was issued on February 28 covering January 1 through December 31 of the prior year. In April, a user entity's IS auditor discovers that the service organization experienced a major system breach in November of the covered year — an event that neither appears in the SOC 2 report nor was disclosed by the service organization. This is a 'subsequently discovered fact.' What are the service auditor's professional obligations?

answers.text: The service auditor has no obligations — the report has been issued and the engagement is complete; subsequently discovered facts after report issuance are beyond the service auditor's responsibility

The service auditor must investigate the subsequently discovered fact: if the breach occurred during the covered period and was known to management but not disclosed to the service auditor, this represents a representation failure; the service auditor should assess whether the report would have differed if the breach had been known; if so, the service auditor should take steps including contacting management, potentially reissuing the report, and notifying known users that the original report should not be relied upon
The service auditor should notify only the user entity that discovered the breach — other users of the report do not need to be informed
The service auditor should retroactively backdate a new report to include the breach finding — backdating corrects the historical record

explanations.a: Professional standards establish obligations for subsequently discovered facts that arise after report issuance. AT-C Section 205 addresses the service auditor's responsibilities when facts discovered after report issuance indicate the report may be misleading.
explanations.b: Subsequently discovered facts — professional obligations: (1) Investigation: the service auditor must investigate whether: the breach actually occurred during the covered period (November — yes, within January 1 – December 31); management knew about the breach during or before the engagement; the breach was a material event that should have been identified during testing or disclosed by management; (2) Assessment: if management knew about the breach and failed to disclose it to the service auditor, they misled the service auditor — the management representations may have been false; had the service auditor known, the report would likely have included the breach as a significant exception; (3) Obligations if the report is materially misleading: notify management and request they address the situation; if management doesn't cooperate, notify persons known to be relying on the report (current users of the SOC 2) that the report should not be relied upon; consider whether to reissue a revised report; notify regulatory authorities if appropriate; (4) Cannot simply ignore: a service auditor who discovers a material misrepresentation in an issued report and does nothing may face professional liability for continued representation of a misleading report.
explanations.c: Restricting notification to one user entity would leave all other users of the report relying on a potentially misleading document. Professional standards require notification of all known users when a report is materially misleading.
explanations.d: Backdating reports is fraudulent — it creates a false historical record. Revised reports are issued with a new date and clearly indicate they replace the original; they are not backdated to appear as if they were originally correct.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts — impact on SOC 1 and SOC 2 engagements
questions.text: A service organization's SOC 1 Type 2 engagement covers July 1 through June 30. Shortly before the report is issued in August, the service organization announces it is acquiring a major competitor and will be integrating the competitor's infrastructure into its own over the next 18 months. The service auditor must evaluate how to address this announcement. Which assessment is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: The acquisition announcement requires immediate re-performance of all testing — the acquisition changes the service organization's system and all prior test results are invalid

The acquisition announcement is a subsequent event that occurred after the period end (June 30) but before report issuance — the service auditor should evaluate the potential impact on user entities and determine whether disclosure is warranted; since the integration hasn't begun, the covered period's controls remain valid; however, if the acquisition represents a material change to the service organization's future operations that user entities would consider significant for their reliance decisions, a subsequent event disclosure may be appropriate to inform them of this material change
Subsequent events of a business nature (acquisitions, mergers) are outside the scope of SOC 1 reporting — only technical control failures are reportable subsequent events
The report cannot be issued until the acquisition is complete — the service auditor must wait until the integration is finished to evaluate controls over the combined entity

explanations.a: The acquisition announcement does not invalidate the test results for July 1 – June 30 — the controls operated as they did during that period regardless of the future acquisition. Re-performance of all testing would be disproportionate and unnecessary.
explanations.b: Subsequent event assessment for business events: (1) Period control validity: the test results for July 1 – June 30 reflect how controls operated during that specific period — the acquisition announcement does not change what happened during the covered period; (2) Subsequent event significance assessment: is this acquisition material? An acquisition of a major competitor with 18-month integration is highly material; would user entities consider this significant to their reliance decision? Yes — integration changes the service organization's system, personnel, processes, and risk profile; does this affect the user entities' ongoing use of the service? Yes — the system they rely on will change significantly; (3) Disclosure decision: the service auditor should include a subsequent event disclosure noting: the acquisition announcement; the expected integration timeline; that the covered period's controls operated as described and were unaffected by the acquisition; and that user entities should consider the future integration in their ongoing assessment of the service; (4) Forward-looking framing: the disclosure informs without invalidating — it helps user entities understand that the service environment is changing, enabling them to plan for the next SOC period.
explanations.c: Business events (acquisitions, leadership changes, major contracts) can be material subsequent events in SOC engagements if they significantly affect user entities' ability to rely on the service organization or the conclusions in the SOC report. The scope is not limited to technical control failures.
explanations.d: Waiting 18 months for integration completion before issuing the report would render the SOC 1 useless for user entities who need it for their current audit cycles. Subsequent event disclosure provides the appropriate mechanism to inform users without delaying issuance.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Effect of complementary user entity controls (CUECs) on the SOC 1 and SOC 2 report
questions.text: A service organization's SOC 1 Type 2 report includes a section listing complementary user entity controls (CUECs) that the service organization assumes user entities will implement. A user entity's auditor is reviewing how these CUECs affect reliance on the report. What is the correct treatment of CUECs in the service auditor's report?

answers.text: The service auditor does not test CUECs, and the opinion is expressed on the basis that the control objectives are achieved only if the CUECs are suitably designed and operating effectively at user entities
The service auditor tests the CUECs at a sample of user entities and includes the results in the description of tests of controls
CUECs replace the service organization's own controls for the related objectives and become the only controls the service auditor evaluates
CUECs are excluded from the description entirely because they are the responsibility of user entities and have no bearing on the report

explanations.a: Correct. CUECs are controls the service organization assumes user entities implement; the service auditor does not test them, and the opinion is conditioned on those CUECs being suitably designed and operating effectively at user entities.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The service auditor performs no procedures at user entities and does not test CUECs; responsibility rests with the user entities.
explanations.c: Incorrect. CUECs supplement rather than replace the service organization's own controls, which are still described and tested.
explanations.d: Incorrect. CUECs must be identified in the description so user entities understand which controls they must implement.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Effect of complementary user entity controls (CUECs) on the SOC 1 and SOC 2 report
questions.text: During a SOC 2 examination, the service organization's system description identifies several complementary user entity controls related to user access provisioning. The service auditor is determining the appropriate way to address these CUECs in the report. Which action is appropriate?

answers.text: Issue a qualified opinion solely because CUECs exist, since their presence indicates the service organization's controls are incomplete
Evaluate whether the CUECs are described clearly enough for user entities to understand and implement them, without testing their operating effectiveness
Test the design and operating effectiveness of each CUEC at the service organization's premises
Remove the CUECs from the description so the opinion can cover all relevant controls without exception

explanations.a: Incorrect. The existence of CUECs is normal and does not by itself warrant a modified opinion.
explanations.b: Correct. The service auditor evaluates whether CUECs are described well enough for user entities to implement them, but does not test CUEC operating effectiveness because they operate at user entities.
explanations.c: Incorrect. CUECs operate at user entities, not the service organization, and are outside the scope of the service auditor's tests.
explanations.d: Incorrect. CUECs must remain in the description; removing them would mislead users about controls they must implement.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Effect of complementary user entity controls (CUECs) on the SOC 1 and SOC 2 report
questions.text: A user entity relies on a payroll service organization and reads in the SOC 1 report that a control objective for accurate payroll depends on a CUEC requiring the user entity to review and approve payroll registers before disbursement. The user entity did not perform this review during the period. What is the implication for the user entity's auditor?

answers.text: The service organization's SOC 1 opinion is automatically invalidated for that control objective
There is no implication, because the service auditor already tested the payroll review on the user entity's behalf

The related control objective may not be met for this user entity, so its auditor cannot rely on the service organization's controls alone and must consider the resulting risk of material misstatement
The user entity should request that the service auditor reissue the report excluding the CUEC

explanations.a: Incorrect. The service organization's opinion is not invalidated; the report explicitly conditions the objective on the CUEC.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The service auditor does not test CUECs at user entities; the review is the user entity's responsibility.
explanations.c: Correct. When a user entity does not implement a CUEC on which an objective depends, that objective may not be achieved for it; the user auditor must consider the increased risk of material misstatement.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The report is not reissued; CUECs are a standard, required element of the description.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Effect of complementary user entity controls (CUECs) on the SOC 1 and SOC 2 report
questions.text: A service auditor completing a SOC 2 Type 2 engagement finds that management's description omits a complementary user entity control essential for meeting the processing integrity criteria, even though the service organization's own controls were suitably designed and operating effectively. Management declines to add the omitted CUEC. How should the service auditor most appropriately respond?

answers.text: Issue an unmodified opinion because the service organization's own controls operated effectively
Withdraw from the engagement immediately, as an omitted CUEC always constitutes a scope limitation
Add the CUEC to the description on the service organization's behalf and issue an unmodified opinion
Conclude the description does not meet the description criteria and modify the opinion (qualified or adverse) because the omission could mislead users about controls they must implement

explanations.a: Incorrect. Effective operation of the service organization's own controls does not cure a materially incomplete description.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Withdrawal is not required; the appropriate response is a modified opinion on the description.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The service auditor cannot author management's description; the description is management's responsibility.
explanations.d: Correct. Omitting an essential CUEC means the description fails the description criteria, warranting a qualified or adverse opinion depending on pervasiveness, even though the service organization's own controls operated effectively.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Carve-out vs. inclusive method of reporting on complementary subservice organization controls (CSOCs)
questions.text: A service organization uses a cloud hosting subservice organization and prepares its SOC 2 report using the carve-out method. A reader wants to understand how the subservice organization is presented. Under the carve-out method, how are the subservice organization's controls treated?

answers.text: They are included in the service organization's description and tested by the service auditor

They are excluded from the description and the service auditor's tests, but the description identifies the subservice organization's functions and the types of complementary subservice organization controls
The subservice organization must issue its own opinion that is bound into the service organization's report
They are described in detail but the service auditor disclaims any opinion on the entire report

explanations.a: Incorrect. That describes the inclusive method, not the carve-out method.
explanations.b: Correct. Carve-out excludes the subservice organization's controls from the description and testing scope, while the description still identifies its functions and the expected complementary subservice organization controls (CSOCs).
explanations.c: Incorrect. No separate bound opinion from the subservice organization is required under the carve-out method.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The service auditor still opines on the service organization's system; only the subservice organization's controls are carved out.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Carve-out vs. inclusive method of reporting on complementary subservice organization controls (CSOCs)
questions.text: A service organization wants its SOC 1 report to cover the controls of a critical subservice organization that performs transaction processing. The service auditor is explaining the requirements of the inclusive method. Which requirement must be satisfied to use the inclusive method?

answers.text: The subservice organization's controls may be included without its knowledge as long as the service organization describes them
The inclusive method may only be used when the subservice organization is a related party of the service organization

The subservice organization must provide its own written assertion and representations, and its controls must be described and subjected to the service auditor's tests alongside the service organization's controls
The service auditor must issue two separate reports, one for the service organization and one for the subservice organization

explanations.a: Incorrect. The subservice organization must actively participate and provide its own assertion; it cannot be included without involvement.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A related-party relationship is not a condition for using the inclusive method.
explanations.c: Correct. The inclusive method incorporates the subservice organization's controls into the description and tests, which requires its own written assertion and representations and its participation.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The inclusive method produces a single combined report, not two separate reports.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Carve-out vs. inclusive method of reporting on complementary subservice organization controls (CSOCs)
questions.text: A prospective user entity compares two service organizations: one issues a SOC 2 report using the carve-out method for its data center subservice organization, and the other uses the inclusive method. The user entity's auditor is assessing the additional procedures required under each method. Which statement best describes the difference in the user entity auditor's responsibilities?

answers.text: Both methods give the user entity's auditor identical assurance over the subservice organization, so no difference in procedures exists
Under the inclusive method the user entity's auditor must separately obtain a SOC report directly from the subservice organization
Under the carve-out method the service auditor has already tested the subservice organization's controls, so no further consideration is needed

Under carve-out the user entity's auditor must separately evaluate the carved-out subservice organization (e.g., obtain its own SOC report), whereas under the inclusive method that coverage is already within the service auditor's report

explanations.a: Incorrect. The two methods provide materially different coverage of the subservice organization.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Under the inclusive method the subservice organization is already covered; a separate report is not required.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Under the carve-out method the service auditor did not test the subservice organization's controls.
explanations.d: Correct. Carve-out excludes the subservice organization from the service auditor's tests, so the user auditor must obtain separate assurance over it; the inclusive method already covers those controls.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Carve-out vs. inclusive method of reporting on complementary subservice organization controls (CSOCs)
questions.text: A service organization's SOC 2 description uses the carve-out method but fails to identify the complementary subservice organization controls the subservice organization is expected to perform for the security criteria to be met. The service auditor confirms the service organization's own controls are suitably designed and operating effectively. What is the most appropriate conclusion?

answers.text: The description does not meet the description criteria because omitting the CSOCs prevents users from understanding controls the subservice organization must perform, warranting a modified opinion despite the effectiveness of the service organization's own controls
An unmodified opinion is appropriate because the carve-out method permits the subservice organization's controls to be omitted entirely
The service auditor must convert the engagement to the inclusive method before issuing any opinion
The omission is immaterial because subservice organization controls are never relevant to the security criteria

explanations.a: Correct. Even under carve-out the description must identify the types of CSOCs expected; omitting them is a description-criteria deficiency warranting a modified opinion regardless of the service organization's own control effectiveness.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Carve-out permits excluding the subservice organization's controls from testing, but the CSOCs must still be identified in the description.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The method need not be converted; the deficiency is in the description's completeness.
explanations.d: Incorrect. CSOCs can be highly relevant to meeting the security criteria.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Types of opinions and report modifications when control deficiencies are identified
questions.text: A service auditor performing a SOC 1 Type 2 engagement identifies a control that was not operating effectively for part of the period; the resulting deficiency affects one control objective but is not pervasive to the description and controls as a whole. Which type of opinion is most appropriate?

answers.text: An unmodified opinion, because Type 2 reports never reflect operating-effectiveness deficiencies
A disclaimer of opinion, because any operating deficiency prevents the formation of an opinion
A qualified opinion, because the deficiency is material to one control objective but not pervasive to the description and controls as a whole
An adverse opinion, because any single ineffective control requires an adverse conclusion

explanations.a: Incorrect. Type 2 opinions do cover operating effectiveness and reflect such deficiencies.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A disclaimer relates to a scope limitation preventing sufficient evidence, not to an identified deficiency.
explanations.c: Correct. A qualified ('except for') opinion fits a material but non-pervasive deficiency; an adverse opinion is reserved for pervasive matters.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Adverse opinions are reserved for pervasive matters, not a single non-pervasive deficiency.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Types of opinions and report modifications when control deficiencies are identified
questions.text: A service auditor is engaged for a SOC 2 Type 1 examination. Management's description fairly presents the system, but the service auditor determines that several controls are not suitably designed to meet the security criteria, and the issue is pervasive. Which opinion is appropriate?

answers.text: An unmodified opinion, because Type 1 engagements only address the description and never the suitability of design
A qualified opinion, because design deficiencies can never be considered pervasive in a Type 1 report
A disclaimer of opinion, because the service auditor could not obtain evidence about design
An adverse opinion, because the controls are not suitably designed to achieve the criteria and the matter is pervasive

explanations.a: Incorrect. A Type 1 opinion does cover suitability of design, not just the description.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Design deficiencies can be pervasive; pervasiveness drives qualified vs. adverse.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A disclaimer arises from inability to obtain evidence, not from an identified pervasive design deficiency.
explanations.d: Correct. A Type 1 report opines on the description and suitability of design; pervasive design deficiencies that prevent the criteria from being met warrant an adverse opinion.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Types of opinions and report modifications when control deficiencies are identified
questions.text: Midway through a SOC 1 Type 2 engagement, the service organization cannot provide evidence supporting the operation of controls for a three-month gap in the examination period, and no alternative procedures are available. The scope limitation is significant and pervasive. What is the most appropriate report outcome?

answers.text: A disclaimer of opinion, because the service auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effects are pervasive
An unmodified opinion with an other-matter paragraph describing the missing evidence
A qualified opinion, because scope limitations are never severe enough to disclaim
An adverse opinion, because missing evidence indicates the controls failed

explanations.a: Correct. A pervasive scope limitation that prevents sufficient appropriate evidence, with no alternative procedures, results in a disclaimer of opinion.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A pervasive evidence limitation cannot be addressed with only an other-matter paragraph.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A pervasive scope limitation does warrant a disclaimer, not merely a qualification.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Absence of evidence is not evidence that controls failed; it is a scope limitation.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Types of opinions and report modifications when control deficiencies are identified
questions.text: A service auditor identifies that management's SOC 2 system description contains a statement about subservice organization monitoring that is not fairly stated, while the controls themselves are suitably designed and operating effectively. The misstatement is material but confined to that single area and is not pervasive. How should the service auditor structure the report?

answers.text: Issue an unmodified opinion, since control operating effectiveness outweighs description accuracy
Issue a qualified opinion on the description ('except for' the misstated subservice monitoring statement) while the opinions on suitability of design and operating effectiveness may remain unmodified
Issue an adverse opinion on the entire report because any description misstatement is pervasive by definition
Issue a disclaimer because conflicting conclusions on the description and the controls cannot be reported together

explanations.a: Incorrect. A material description misstatement cannot be ignored because controls operated effectively.
explanations.b: Correct. SOC 2 opinions address the description, design, and operating effectiveness; a material but non-pervasive description misstatement warrants a qualified opinion on the description while the other opinions can remain unmodified.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A confined, non-pervasive misstatement warrants a qualified, not adverse, opinion.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The report can express differentiated conclusions across the description and the controls.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Presenting results of tests of controls in a SOC 2 report, including testing exceptions
questions.text: A SOC 2 Type 2 report includes a section prepared by the service auditor describing the controls, the tests performed, and the results of those tests. A reader asks what this section must contain when all tests passed. Which content is required in the description of tests of controls?

answers.text: Only a summary statement that all controls operated effectively, with no detail of procedures
The internal audit workpapers of the service organization reproduced in full
A list of user entities that relied on the report during the period
The controls tested, the nature of the service auditor's tests, and the results of those tests

explanations.a: Incorrect. A bare summary without describing the procedures is insufficient for a Type 2 report.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The service organization's internal audit workpapers are not reproduced in the report.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A list of relying user entities is not a required element of the test results section.
explanations.d: Correct. For a Type 2 SOC 2 report the service auditor presents the controls, the nature of the tests, and the results so users understand the basis for the opinion.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Presenting results of tests of controls in a SOC 2 report, including testing exceptions
questions.text: During a SOC 2 Type 2 examination, the service auditor tests a change-management control over 25 selected changes and finds 2 changes deployed without documented approval. The service auditor concludes the processing integrity criteria were still met overall. How should this be presented in the report?

answers.text: Describe the test, the number of items tested and the number and nature of exceptions, and the service auditor's evaluation, even though the related criteria were ultimately met
Omit the exceptions entirely because the criteria were met overall
Automatically issue a qualified opinion because any exception requires a modified opinion
Replace the test results with management's explanation of why the exceptions occurred, without the service auditor's own conclusion

explanations.a: Correct. Identified exceptions are disclosed in the test results — the number tested, the number and nature of exceptions, and the service auditor's evaluation — even when the criteria were still met overall.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Exceptions are disclosed even when the criteria are met overall; transparency is required.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Not every exception requires a modified opinion; the opinion depends on whether the criteria were met.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The report presents the service auditor's evaluation, not solely management's explanation.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Presenting results of tests of controls in a SOC 2 report, including testing exceptions
questions.text: A service auditor's SOC 2 Type 2 testing reveals that an access-review control failed throughout the period such that the security criteria were not met; the deficiency is material but not pervasive to the system as a whole. The service organization provides a written management response explaining the deficiency. Which presentation is appropriate?

answers.text: Present only management's response and issue an unmodified opinion since management acknowledged the issue

Disclose the exception and the service auditor's conclusion that the criteria were not met, issue a qualified opinion, and present management's response as a separate, clearly labeled section not covered by the opinion
Move the deficiency out of the report and into a private letter to management to avoid alarming users
Issue an adverse opinion because any access-control failure is inherently pervasive

explanations.a: Incorrect. Management's acknowledgment does not cure a deficiency or justify an unmodified opinion.
explanations.b: Correct. A material, non-pervasive failure means the criteria were not met: it is disclosed in the test results and leads to a qualified opinion, with management's response presented separately and clearly identified as not covered by the opinion.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The deficiency must be disclosed in the report, not concealed in a private letter.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A non-pervasive failure warrants a qualified opinion, not an adverse one.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Presenting results of tests of controls in a SOC 2 report, including testing exceptions
questions.text: In a SOC 2 Type 2 report, the service auditor tested a monitoring control and identified an exception, but additional procedures showed a compensating control operated effectively so the applicable trust services criteria were still met. The service organization argues the exception should be excluded because the criteria were ultimately satisfied. What is the most appropriate course of action?

answers.text: Exclude the exception, since the compensating control means no user-relevant information was lost
Issue a qualified opinion because the presence of any compensating control signals an unreliable system
Disclose the original exception, the compensating control, and the additional procedures performed, then express an unmodified opinion because the criteria were met
Disclaim an opinion because reliance on a compensating control prevents a clear conclusion

explanations.a: Incorrect. Exceptions are disclosed even when compensating controls remediate the effect.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A compensating control that achieves the criteria supports an unmodified opinion, not a qualification.
explanations.c: Correct. Transparency requires disclosing the exception, the compensating control, and the additional procedures; because the criteria were met, an unmodified opinion is appropriate while still informing users.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A disclaimer relates to evidence limitations, not to satisfactory results achieved via a compensating control.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Form and content of the service auditor's report on controls at a service organization (SOC 1, SOC 2)
questions.text: A service auditor is finalizing a SOC 1 Type 2 report and is confirming the elements it must contain. A staff member asks which restriction on use applies. Which statement about the SOC 1 report's use is correct?

answers.text: The SOC 1 report is restricted to use by management of the service organization, user entities, and the auditors of those user entities
The SOC 1 report is a general-use report freely distributable to the public, like a SOC 3 report
The SOC 1 report may be used by anyone who signs a nondisclosure agreement with the subservice organization
The SOC 1 report has no restricted-use paragraph because its subject matter is financial reporting

explanations.a: Correct. A SOC 1 report is restricted to the service organization's management, user entities, and the auditors of those user entities, who have sufficient knowledge of the system.
explanations.b: Incorrect. SOC 1 is restricted-use; SOC 3 is the general-use report.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Use is restricted to specified parties, not anyone with an NDA with a subservice organization.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The restricted-use paragraph is a required element of a SOC 1 report.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Form and content of the service auditor's report on controls at a service organization (SOC 1, SOC 2)
questions.text: A service auditor is drafting a SOC 2 Type 2 report and the engagement partner reviews the draft to confirm all required elements are present. Which combination of elements must a SOC 2 Type 2 report include?

answers.text: Only the service auditor's opinion and the date, since the description and tests are optional in Type 2 reports

Management's assertion, the system description, the service auditor's opinion covering the description, suitability of design and operating effectiveness, the description of tests of controls and results, and a restricted-use statement
A general-use distribution statement and a list of every control framework available in the industry
The service organization's audited financial statements and the user entities' internal control narratives

explanations.a: Incorrect. The description and the tests of controls are required elements of a Type 2 report, not optional.
explanations.b: Correct. A SOC 2 Type 2 report includes management's assertion, the system description, the service auditor's opinion (description, suitability of design, operating effectiveness), the tests of controls and results, and a restricted-use statement.
explanations.c: Incorrect. SOC 2 is restricted-use, and an exhaustive list of industry frameworks is not a report element.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Financial statements and user entity narratives are not components of a SOC 2 report.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Form and content of the service auditor's report on controls at a service organization (SOC 1, SOC 2)
questions.text: A user entity's auditor compares a SOC 1 Type 1 report with a SOC 1 Type 2 report from the same service organization and needs to know which report supports reliance on operating effectiveness for the audit of the user entity's financial statements. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: Both Type 1 and Type 2 reports support reliance on operating effectiveness because both cover a period of time
The Type 1 report supports reliance on operating effectiveness because it is dated as of a point in time

Only the Type 2 report supports reliance on operating effectiveness, because it covers suitability of design and operating effectiveness over a specified period, whereas the Type 1 report addresses design as of a specified date only
Neither report can support reliance on operating effectiveness; the user entity's auditor must always test the service organization's controls directly

explanations.a: Incorrect. A Type 1 report is as of a point in time and does not cover operating effectiveness over a period.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Being dated as of a point in time is precisely why a Type 1 report does not support operating-effectiveness reliance.
explanations.c: Correct. A Type 1 report addresses the description and suitability of design as of a date; only a Type 2 report covers operating effectiveness over a period and can support reliance on operating effectiveness.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A Type 2 report can support reliance, reducing or eliminating the need to test the service organization's controls directly.

questions.name: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
questions.keyword: Form and content of the service auditor's report on controls at a service organization (SOC 1, SOC 2)
questions.text: A service auditor must decide the form and content of the opinion paragraph for a SOC 1 Type 2 engagement in which controls were suitably designed and operating effectively, but the description omits a significant subservice organization that was carved out without identifying its functions. The service auditor concludes the omission is material but not pervasive. How should the opinion paragraph be structured?

answers.text: An unmodified opinion on all three matters, because the controls tested were effective
A disclaimer of opinion, because a description omission always prevents an opinion
An adverse opinion on the entire report, because omitting a subservice organization is inherently pervasive

A qualified opinion 'except for' the description's failure to identify the carved-out subservice organization's functions, while the opinions on suitability of design and operating effectiveness remain unmodified

explanations.a: Incorrect. Effective controls do not cure a material description omission.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A disclaimer relates to evidence limitations, not to an identified description omission.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A non-pervasive omission warrants a qualified, not adverse, opinion.
explanations.d: Correct. The description must identify carved-out subservice organization functions; a material but non-pervasive omission warrants a qualified ('except for') opinion on the description while the design and operating-effectiveness opinions remain unmodified.
